overall: The article's biggest weakness is that it occasionally overstates findings into absolute claims—such as asserting that continuing a losing SIP beat stopping 'every time' and phrasing takeaways as prescriptive financial advice—while omitting mandated nuances like drawdown depth breakdowns and the critique comparison to Japan. Its biggest strength is its rigorous, rupee-denominated empirical framework that transparently tests popular investing heuristics and exposes the severe historical penalty of pausing or stopping instalments during market drawdowns.

answers.q1: A Nifty 500 SIP lost money in 29% of one-year windows, 16% of three-year windows, 7% of five-year windows, and 0% of ten-year windows (with no start month losing from eight years on), while trailing a taxed fixed deposit in 38%, 25%, 16%, and 0.4% of windows respectively, and trailing inflation in 0.8% of ten-year windows.
answers.q2: Ten-year Nifty 500 SIPs returned a median of 14.6% a year across a wide range (5th percentile 9.8%, worst 4.3%, best 32.7%), with ₹10,000 monthly over 20 years typically yielding ₹1.30 crore (ranging from ₹1.00 crore to ₹1.54 crore).
answers.q3: After inflation, the typical ten-year Nifty 500 SIP earned 8.4% a year (with 5% of periods earning under 2.0% and 0.8% losing purchasing power), whereas a taxed fixed deposit lost 0.7 percentage points a year to inflation.
answers.q4: Over ten years from 2005, mid caps had the highest median (17.9%) and bad-case (12.0%) returns, small caps had high medians (15.3%) but lost money in their worst start (-0.5%) with a 54% maximum fall, the Nifty 500 returned 13.5% (bad case 9.3%), and government bonds returned 8.0% with only a 4% maximum fall.
answers.q5: Over ten years, a 60/20/20 mix gave up ₹1.4 lakh of median final value to gain ₹0.2 lakh at the 5th percentile while reducing the worst drawdown from 44% to 25%, whereas over 5 and 15 years the bad-case rupee gain exceeded the median rupee sacrificed.
answers.q6: Rebalancing a 60/20/20 SIP each April added a median 0.8 percentage points a year over ten years and improved returns in at least nine in ten start months.
answers.q7: Longer SIP horizons compressed the 5th-to-95th percentile spread of annualised returns from 41 percentage points at five years to 3.5 points at twenty years, yet the 20-year rupee multiple still ranged widely between 4.2 and 6.4 times total contributions.
answers.q8: The starting year caused ten-year median returns to range widely from 9.3% in 2010 to 26.5% in 1997, whereas starting near a market peak versus 10% below it made almost no difference (13.6% versus 14.9%).
answers.q9: The first five years of instalments accounted for 55% of a 15-year SIP's final value, and switching the portfolio to fixed deposits over the final 36 months ended ahead in only 19% of start months while lowering the 5th-percentile corpus from ₹43.8 lakh to ₹39.5 lakh.
answers.q10: Reaching ₹1 crore in 15 years required monthly contributions of ₹16,455 for 50% confidence, ₹19,459 for 80% confidence, and ₹22,810 for 95% confidence (versus ₹21,011 from a 12% calculator), while delaying by five years forced contributions to jump to ₹21,612 a month.
answers.q11: For an investor with an existing lump sum, investing immediately beat a 12-month STP in 57% of start months; for a salaried saver, monthly SIPs beat saving in an FD and investing annually in 73% of start months.
answers.q12: Execution dates, weekly frequency, and valuation rules altered 10-year returns by 0.2 percentage points or less, whereas pausing during a 20% crash or incurring a 1% higher expense ratio reduced annual returns by 1.1 to 3.8 percentage points.
answers.q13: A SIP is never fully long-term while active because each monthly instalment resets its own one-year clock; at two years, 50% of units remain short-term (holding 27% of gains), and redemption costs fluctuate as exit loads lapse and gains exceed the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption.
answers.q14: Volatility did not reliably enhance SIP results, showing only a 0.23 rank correlation with the SIP's return edge over the buy-and-hold index (and −0.05 after 2005) because extra units bought during dips were counterbalanced by expensive units bought at peaks.
answers.q15: Nearly all Nifty 500 SIPs (97%) experienced underwater periods, enduring a maximum drawdown of 44% below invested capital and a longest continuous underwater stretch of 38 months.
answers.q16: Nifty 500 SIPs in the red after 12 months achieved higher median 10-year returns than those in the black (17.9% versus 14.1%) because the 18% of money deployed while underwater acquired 30% of total units, though this bonus did not materialize in mid caps.
answers.q17: For Nifty 500 SIPs in the red at 12 months, continuing instalments beat stopping, switching to FDs, or pausing in 100% of historical start months (saving a median ₹1.4 lakh to ₹14.8 lakh), although in small caps stopping beat continuing in 11% of cases.
answers.q18: A SIP's running return is uninformative or slightly misleading early in its life (showing a −0.35 correlation with final 10-year returns at 12 months) and does not surpass a 0.5 correlation until 99 months.
answers.q19: Historical Nifty 50 SIPs in the red at 12 months finished similarly whether trailing P/E was low or high (14.8% versus 14.3%), while currently Nifty 50 P/E stands at its 35th percentile and deposit rates at their 25th percentile.
answers.q20: Aggregate SIP inflows did not exhibit adverse timing; when compared against a benchmark growing at the inflows' 23% annual trend, actual investor cash flows trailed by only 0.1 percentage points (11.2% versus 11.3%).
answers.q21: Market drawdowns were somewhat shallower after 2016 (median fall of 16% versus 20% prior to 2016), but ten years of data is insufficient to prove that SIP inflows caused this moderation.
answers.q22: Based on AMFI closure data, the implied average lifespan of a SIP account is roughly 1.8 years (and has never exceeded 4.9 years outside cleanups), while the April 2025 closure spike to 3.5 times registrations was a dormant account cleanup artifact.

issues.quote: no ten-year SIP lost money, and keeping a losing SIP going beat stopping it every time.
issues.problem: Claiming that keeping a losing SIP going beat stopping 'every time' overstates the findings, as small-cap SIPs that stopped beat continuing in 11% of start months and 24-month red Nifty 500 SIPs beat continuing in 1.6% of cases.
issues.fix: Qualify the claim to specify that continuing beat stopping in 100% of cases for Nifty 500 SIPs in the red after 12 months under baseline deposit assumptions.

issues.quote: Stopping at that point, in every case in this record, left people worse off, often by lakhs of rupees.
issues.problem: The summary takeaway read alone overclaims by stating stopping left people worse off 'in every case in this record', contradicting the study's own small-cap and 24-month findings.
issues.fix: Rewrite to: 'For broad large-cap index SIPs in the red after a year, stopping at that point consistently left savers worse off across this record, often by lakhs of rupees.'

issues.quote: Don't spend energy on the date of your SIP or clever timing rules: they barely matter. Spend it on choosing something broad and cheap, and on not stopping when it hurts.
issues.problem: Phrasing research findings as imperative directives ('Don't spend energy...', 'Spend it on choosing...') constitutes direct financial advice rather than empirical reporting.
issues.evidence: Plan: 'anything that reads as a forecast or advice'
issues.fix: Rephrase descriptively: 'The historical record indicates that savers gained little from optimizing dates or timing rules, while fund asset choice and staying invested through drawdowns had far larger impacts on final wealth.'

issues.quote: Two stories went around at once. One said SIPs never lose over the long run, so ignore it. The other said SIP is broken: the success stories came from cheap markets and 12% deposits, and they won't repeat.
issues.problem: The draft omits international lost decades (specifically Japan), which the plan explicitly required as the critique in its strongest form.
issues.evidence: Plan section 'Questions I won't ask': 'Other countries' lost decades (Japan): index licences not cleared. Mentioned in words only, as the critique's strongest example.'
issues.fix: Add a passage in Chapter 6 or the caveats explicitly citing Japan's multi-decade equity stagnation as the critique's primary historical example where cost averaging took decades to break even.

issues.quote: Did stopping a SIP that was in the red protect the investor? Never. For each of the 83 Nifty 500 start months since 1995 that were in the red at 12 months
issues.problem: The draft fails to report the planned estimand and second figure examining the rupee cost of stopping broken down by drawdown depth bands, omitting the reason why prediction P17 failed.
issues.evidence: Plan Q17 estimand, Prediction P17, and results keys q17_n500_m12_gap_C_p50_shallow vs q17_n500_m12_gap_C_p50_deep
issues.fix: Incorporate the depth band results into Q17, explaining that the median cost of moving to FDs was actually higher for shallow drawdowns (₹13.8 lakh) than for deep drawdowns over 20% (₹10.3 lakh).

issues.quote: That edge correlated only weakly with how volatile the window was (rank correlation 0.23), and for SIPs started after 2005 not at all (−0.05).
issues.problem: The draft omits the planned estimand comparing the SIP edge's correlation with the window's total return (-0.18), obscuring the testing of Prediction P14.
issues.evidence: Plan Q14 estimand, Prediction P14, and results keys q14_n500_corr_total (-0.177) and q14_P14_holds (False)
issues.fix: State the Spearman correlation between the SIP edge and the window's total return (-0.18), noting that contrary to prediction P14, the edge correlated slightly more with volatility across the full history, though both effects diminished after 2005.

issues.quote: With a lump sum in hand, investing it at once beat a 12-month STP in 57% of start months.
issues.problem: The abbreviation 'STP' is used in the chart caption without ever being spelled out or explained in the text.
issues.evidence: Draft Figure F.q11 caption and Section Q11
issues.fix: Define STP on first mention as 'a Systematic Transfer Plan (STP), where a lump sum sits in a debt fund and moves into equity in monthly instalments'.

issues.quote: Doubling the instalment when the Nifty 50's P/E was in the cheapest fifth of its history changed nothing
issues.problem: The financial ratio 'P/E' is introduced without explaining what a price-to-earnings ratio measures.
issues.fix: Define P/E on first use: 'price-to-earnings ratio (P/E, a valuation measure comparing stock prices to underlying company earnings)'.

issues.quote: Their statement said it was worth about ₹1.08 lakh: 10% down, and an XIRR, the annualised return the app shows, of −18% a year.
issues.problem: The acronym 'XIRR' is used without defining what it stands for or clarifying how it measures money-weighted returns across periodic instalments.
issues.fix: Expand the first mention: 'an XIRR (extended internal rate of return, the standard calculation apps use to annualise returns across multiple dated cash flows)'.

issues.quote: Waiting in an FD for 20% falls and investing then added a median 1.2 points, but it rests on two crashes (2008 and 2020) and lost in at least one start month in ten. <Figure {...F.q12_days} />
issues.problem: Figure F.q12_days (showing returns across days 1 to 28 of the month) is placed directly after text discussing waiting for 20% falls rather than near the paragraph discussing SIP dates.
issues.evidence: Draft Section Q12 and Figures list F.q12_days
issues.fix: Move Figure F.q12_days adjacent to the text discussing day-of-the-month returns, or insert introductory text directly above it.

issues.quote: And ₹1 crore at current prices, after inflation, needed ₹16,042 a month in rupees of the day, four times in five.
issues.problem: Juxtaposing 'at current prices, after inflation' with 'in rupees of the day' creates a confusing phrasing that requires re-reading to understand purchasing power deflations.
issues.fix: Rewrite as: 'Targeting ₹1 crore in today's purchasing power (adjusting historical instalments and the goal for inflation) required ₹16,042 a month four times in five.'

issues.quote: Both stories are about a method, and a SIP is barely a method. It is a way of paying into an investment a little at a time.
issues.problem: The draft omits the exact AMFI count of outstanding SIP accounts, which the approved plan required to be included from the data.
issues.evidence: Plan section 'The big question': 'AMFI counts crores of SIP accounts; the exact count, from the data, goes in the article.'
issues.fix: Include the latest AMFI outstanding SIP account count in the introductory text.

issues.quote: The typical ten-year Nifty 500 SIP returned 8.4% a year after inflation, against 14.6% before it.
issues.problem: The text reports an 8.4% real return, whereas the exact result is 8.35% (rounding down to 8.3%, as correctly shown in Figure F.q3 caption).
issues.fix: Harmonize the text and scorecard to report 8.3% to match the data and figure caption.
